entries.description:
An ordered row of values of any kind, numbered from 0. `New Array()` is empty; `New Array(3)` holds three Undefined elements, ready to be set. A size of 0, a negative one or one that is not a number refuses to create the array. Elements are read by index — `a[0]` or Get — and written by index — `a[0] = x` or Set; an index past the last element raises, for a read and for a write alike: an array grows only by Add and Insert.

Foreach walks the elements in order. A value put into an array is kept as it is — an array, a structure or a table added is that same object, not a copy. Two arrays are equal when their elements are, in order, so an array serves as a compound key of a grouping or a join.

The LINQ operations — Where, Select, OrderBy, First, Any and the rest — apply to an array as to any collection; Sum, Min, Max and Average are the array's own as well.
entries.parameters: size — how many elements the new array holds, each Undefined; a number greater than 0. Left out, the array is empty.

entries.description: How many elements the array holds. The last one is `a[a.Count() - 1]`; an empty array answers 0.
The element at the index, counted from 0 — the same as `a[index]`. An index past the last element raises.
entries.example: First = Items.Get(0);   // the same as Items[0]

entries.description: Appends the value at the end; Count() grows by one. The value is kept as it is: an object added — an array, a structure, a table — is that object, and a change made to it later is seen through the array. Called with no argument, it appends Undefined.
Puts the value BEFORE the element at the index; that element and the ones after it move up by one. An index equal to Count() appends, as Add does; a larger one raises and nothing is inserted.
entries.parameters:
index — the position the value takes, from 0 to Count().
value — any value.

entries.description:
The index of the first element equal to the value, or Undefined when none is. Equality is the language's `=`: 1 and "1" are different values, and two arrays with equal elements are equal.

To ask only WHETHER the value is there, use Contains: the first element's index is 0, and a 0 is not a yes or a no.
entries.parameters: value — what an element must equal.
entries.return_descr: Number — the index from 0; or Undefined.
entries.example: Index = Items.Find("Ink");   // Undefined when no element is "Ink"

entries.description: Removes every element; Count() is then 0.
Writes the value over the element at the index — the same as `a[index] = value`. An index past the last element raises: Set does not grow the array, Add and Insert do.
entries.parameters:
index — the element's position, from 0.
value — any value.
entries.example: Items.Set(0, "Paper A4");   // the same as Items[0] = "Paper A4"

entries.description: Removes the element at the index; the ones after it move down by one. An index past the last element raises and nothing is removed. To remove a VALUE, find its index first.
True when some element equals the value — compared as Find compares — and False otherwise.
entries.parameters: value — what an element must equal.

entries.description:
Puts the elements in order, in place — ascending, or descending when True is passed. Values of one kind compare as that kind does: numbers by size, strings as text, dates by time. Values of different kinds are ordered by their kind first, so a mixed array still sorts, each kind in a run of its own.

To order by something the elements carry rather than by the elements themselves, a query says it: `from l in Lines orderby l.Amount descending select l`.
entries.parameters: descending — True for descending; False or left out for ascending.

entries.description:
Orders this array by a second one: element i of `keys` is the sort key of element i here. This array is reordered; `keys` is left as it was. The two arrays must be of the same length. Keys compare as Sort compares them.

It is the step a LINQ `orderby` takes; in a script, a query usually says the same thing more plainly.
entries.parameters:
keys — an Array of the same length: the key of each element, by position.
descending — True for descending; False or left out for ascending.

entries.description:
Adds the elements up with the language's `+`: numbers are summed exactly (0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3), strings are joined. With a selector — a function of one parameter — each element goes through it first and its results are added, which is how an array of rows or structures is totalled by one of their fields.

An empty array answers Undefined, not 0.
entries.syntax_block:
Total = Prices.Sum();
Total = Lines.Sum(Function(l) { return l.Amount; });
entries.parameters: selector — a function of one parameter that answers with what to add; left out, the elements themselves are added.
entries.return_descr: The sum; Undefined for an empty array.

entries.description: The smallest element, as Sort orders them. With a selector, the smallest of the selector's RESULTS — the value it answered, not the element it was given. An empty array answers Undefined.
entries.syntax_block:
Least = Prices.Min();
Least = Lines.Min(Function(l) { return l.Date; });
entries.parameters: selector — a function of one parameter that answers with what to compare; left out, the elements themselves.
entries.return_descr: The smallest value; Undefined for an empty array.

entries.description: The largest element, as Sort orders them. With a selector, the largest of the selector's RESULTS — the value it answered, not the element it was given. An empty array answers Undefined.
entries.syntax_block:
Most = Prices.Max();
Most = Lines.Max(Function(l) { return l.Amount; });
entries.parameters: selector — a function of one parameter that answers with what to compare; left out, the elements themselves.
entries.return_descr: The largest value; Undefined for an empty array.

entries.description: The sum of the elements divided by their count — for numbers. With a selector, the average of its results. The division is exact, and a fraction that does not end (10 / 3) is carried to 30 digits after the point, so round the result for display. An empty array answers Undefined.
entries.syntax_block:
Mean = Prices.Average();
Mean = Lines.Average(Function(l) { return l.Amount; });
entries.parameters: selector — a function of one parameter that answers with the number to average; left out, the elements themselves.
entries.return_descr: Number; Undefined for an empty array.
